overview: **Simulated snapshot:** these 243 cases are not survey evidence; each scenario assigns one primary private thought group per person.
**Income timing** matters: recorded and prepared fees may shrink before robots can perform live music.
**Paid alternatives** depend on actual customers, wages, qualifications, rooms, and household cash reserves.

S0.headline: Most musicians plan to keep paid work through modest AI change, while existing bills and bookings still matter.

whatTheyDo.text: Zoe Rahman plans to keep teaching six regular pupils and honour booked quartet dates.
Fatima Mensah plans to save one cleared recording fee monthly if choir dates hold.
Priya Baker plans to stop practice-booth rental if hall cancels a paid dance night.
Karl Weber plans to use AI tagging tools to upload four tracks a week instead of three.

whatTheySay: **Live performance** still depends on players, rehearsal, and a paying venue under modest automation.
**Routine software** may shorten booking or editing work, but it does little to guarantee a musician’s next fee.
whatTheyThink: **Existing cash gaps** and unstable contracts matter more than a small new tool for those with thin reserves.
**Booked work and savings** let others absorb one late fee or cancelled date.
howTheyFeel: **Calm** is the largest mood group, with 126 of 243 profiles expecting little change to their current work.
**Anxious** profiles still number 77, often because ordinary lost pay can disrupt household bills.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.94 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.02 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 1.80 among 81 early-career profiles, versus 1.70 among 81 late-career profiles in this 243-source snapshot.

quotes.name: Zoe Rahman
quotes.text: A cancelled wedding can leave rent short even when AI turns out to be mostly hype.

quotes.name: Fatima Mensah
quotes.text: An untidy contract irritates me, but one delayed fee would not change the children’s dinner.

quotes.name: Nora Gupta
quotes.text: A waiting list of eight children is the best problem a piano teacher can have.

thoughts.text: Thin reserves or current bills make routine losses costly.
Existing contracts, buyers, or skills threaten current income.
Current work or savings can weather a small change.
Small software tools already help or affect the work.

S1.headline: Recorded and prepared music fees come under pressure while many live bookings continue.

whatTheyDo.text: Zoe Rahman plans to require deposits for new wedding quartet dates.
Rafael Fischer plans to learn adaptive game-music tools and sell setups to an indie studio.
Fatima Mensah plans to ask musicians’ union for minimum fees and recording reuse consent this month.

Marco Bauer plans a brass class after two cue losses, with written room/hire charges before deposits. Six safe paid places must cover his teaching/preparation, a senior teacher, room, instruments and trains at launch and renewal; otherwise he replaces unsafe gear or defers and refunds everyone.

Wendy Evans plans to apply after both guide and coaching cuts, only to a qualifying posted paid coach role with written replacement net after travel and workable pickup. She keeps paid opera work until a signed offer.

whatTheySay: **Human performance** retains a role at weddings, theatres, churches, and lessons where customers still pay for it.
**AI music tools** raise immediate questions about fees, copyright, and what a client will still commission.
whatTheyThink: **Recording and preparation** provide a meaningful share of pay for many musicians and could lose buyers first.
**Multiple incomes** do not always protect a household when lessons, venue dates, or a partner’s work also weaken.
howTheyFeel: **Anxious** is the dominant response, recorded in 200 of 243 profiles as paid music tasks begin to shift.
**Thin reserves** leave less time to replace a missing commission than moderate or strong savings do.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.35 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.88 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 2.90 among 81 early-career profiles, versus 3.07 among 81 late-career profiles in this 243-source snapshot.

quotes.name: Zoe Rahman
quotes.text: Grocery money comes from little recording fees that a machine could erase before anyone cancels a concert.

quotes.name: Karl Mensah
quotes.text: A producer can stop calling me without dismissing me from the theatre band, and that would still change our savings plan.

quotes.name: Priya Baker
quotes.text: A new tool may help me avoid a wrong note, but it cannot turn an unpaid dance into a wage.

S2.headline: Rapid thinking AI threatens screen-made income by 2028, before capable playing robots arrive around 2031.

whatTheyDo.text: Fatima Mensah plans to apply after 2028 recording orders stop, only to an advertised paid school post accepting her degree and experience, with written net wages covering travel and hours fitting child pickup. She keeps pit work and six pupils until a written offer.
Zoe Rahman plans to call wedding venues about deposits this month.
Jade Ziegler plans to join the union emergency fund and apply for every arts grant.
Karl Mensah plans to stop renting second practice room in first year after 2028 if beat orders halve.
Sara Dubois plans to ask other hotels and restaurants about live piano evenings.

whatTheySay: **Recorded music work** can disappear quickly even while a live player remains useful for a few more years.
**Replacement wages** require real openings and written pay terms; savings alone cannot become lasting income.
whatTheyThink: **Thinking work** such as arranging, editing, and planning can lose buyers before robots can perform on stage.
**Household exposure** grows if lessons, venue spending, or a partner’s wages also fall.
howTheyFeel: **Alarmed** describes 105 profiles and **panicked** another two under rapid AGI.
**Some households** also anticipate losses in lessons, venue spending, or partner wages alongside recorded fees.
**Thin-cushion worry** averages 3.93, versus 3.11 for strong-cushion profiles on the one-to-five mood scale.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.93 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 3.11 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 3.65 among 81 early-career profiles, versus 3.30 among 81 late-career profiles in this 243-source snapshot.

quotes.name: Zoe Rahman
quotes.text: In 2028, an empty recording calendar could arrive three years before any robot picks up a violin.

quotes.name: Fatima Mensah
quotes.text: Our nine-month savings are a bridge, not a replacement wage.

quotes.name: Yusuf Mensah
quotes.text: Losing a third of my pay is enough to make the mortgage sums wake me at night.

S3.headline: Some musicians plan paid alternatives during the five-year runway; many expect fees to erode before or by 2031.

whatTheyDo.text: Lena Ito plans to accept post-2031 rehearsal and guide calls only with written paid hours, consent and recording-reuse fees.
Fatima Mensah plans to start six-week library group with free room, eight prepayments covering teaching/preparation and pickup arranged.
Yusuf Mensah plans to enrol only with funded place, paid hours, no lost income, bus and recognised certificate.
Karl Mensah plans to apply for vacancy first post-2031 year if qualified, beats fall and pay covers travel and mortgage.
Tomas Lopez plans to save half the extra paid adult trumpet-class earnings if a full school term runs.

whatTheySay: **Paid classes** need enough confirmed customers to cover rooms, preparation, teaching, and other musicians.
**Training** is useful when a funded place leads to a recognized skill and a real paid opening.
whatTheyThink: **Screen fees** may shrink before 2031 even with five years of warning and later stage robots around 2034.
**A longer runway** can support a teaching group, live business, or qualification, though paid demand must be tested.
howTheyFeel: **Anxious** remains the clear majority at 218 profiles, even with time to try another earnings route.
**Average worry** is 3.00 under AGI by 2031, versus 3.45 under AGI by 2028.

differences.text: Average worry is 3.11 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 2.90 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 3.10 among 81 resistant profiles, versus 2.94 among 81 adaptive profiles.

quotes.name: Yusuf Mensah

S4.headline: A decade to 2036 gives musicians more time to build paid alternatives, while current fees and bills still count.

whatTheyDo.text: Zoe Rahman plans to keep six pupils and give a term of notice before fee changes.
Fatima Mensah plans to save one cleared recording fee into mortgage reserve when paid.

Priya Baker plans to seek a qualifying posted desk job only after dance-fee cuts, with written replacement net after travel and workable transport hours. She keeps current paid music until a suitable signed offer.

Jade Costa plans a flute circle outside chamber calls, securing written room charges before deposits. Eight safe paid places must cover her teaching/preparation, accompanist, room, cleaned instruments and travel at launch and renewal; otherwise she replaces unsafe flutes or defers and refunds everyone.
Zoe Haddad plans to finish the teaching assistant course within the year.

whatTheySay: **Teaching and live work** can grow during the warning years when families, venues, or pupils actually pay.
**Retirement plans** need verified income; the distant AGI date does not settle today’s mortgage or rent.
whatTheyThink: **Some music fees** may fade well before 2036, while capable playing robots follow around 2039.
**Current savings and contracts** give some musicians room to plan; others still need wages when AGI arrives.
howTheyFeel: **Uneasy and anxious** dominate, with 121 and 106 profiles respectively; only 16 are calm.
**Thin-cushion worry** averages 2.95, above the strong-cushion average of 1.95.

differences.text: Average worry is 2.95 among 81 thin-cushion profiles, versus 1.95 among 81 strong-cushion profiles (1 calm to 5 panicked).
Average worry is 2.20 among 81 early-career profiles, versus 2.38 among 81 late-career profiles in this 243-source snapshot.

quotes.text: I would be 37 when thinking AI arrived in 2036, still young enough to teach but too old to live on promises.

quotes.name: Priya Baker

quotes.name: Yusuf Mensah
quotes.text: Ten years before AGI in 2036 gives me time to check contracts, not a spare month in the bank.
